desc: We have received a reply from the Führer himself, who has accepted all terms of the Treaty Of Riga. All hostilities along the front are to cease, and both German and Russian troops will withdraw from the occupied areas. At long last, the sacrifices of the millions who gave their lives for Russia will no longer be in vain.

title: The Treaty of Riga
desc:
The German Foreign Minister entered the manor, referred to as the House of the Black Heads by local Latvians. He had been sent here by the Führer to do the impossible job of negotiating a 'fair' peace settlement for the Reich, a task he was already sure would be impossible. He kept a scowl on his face, his face glistening with sweat as the rather unfriendly-looking Russian soldiers escorted him to a study. Waiting patiently inside the room was none other than the Federation's most feared general, Alexander Novikov himself.

"You finally made it, German," The Field Marshal spat out the last word, a snarl on his face, his bright blue eyes glaring daggers at the Foreign Minister, akin to that of a wolf stalking its prey.

"I'm sorry, Slav," The Foreign Minister replied, hate in his quivery, laughably high-pitched voice, drawing out the final syllable in an attempt to assert an aura of dominance over the smirking Russian who towered over him a meter away. "I don't like wasting my time with subhumans."

"Very well then!" the general chortled, gesturing to the papers laid out on the table in the middle of the room rather elaborately. "Would you Ubermensch kindly sign the terms of surrender? The war has... not gone well for your side, and I think we both agree it is time for our Motherland's rightful territories to be returned to her. It's not like your forces could ever match up to ours, anyway," Novikov mocked, flashing quite the grin.

He picked up the papers detailing the Treaty of Riga, his hands trembling as he scanned through the terms, his worse fears being confirmed. Brauchitschstadt, Paulusburg, Kiew and Riga. The damned beasts wanted it all back. Unacceptable, every cell in his body screamed, as he put pen to paper, signing the treaty that would cripple Germany forever. Disgraceful! Atrocious! The piece of paper was practically spitting on the Reich's pride, on everything they stood for!

And yet, he had no other choice.

So, the curtains close on this era as the tortured of Russia rejoice. From Murmansk to Omolon, the Baltic to the Bering, their Motherland emerges from the dust once again. However bruised and battered she may be, the treaty is a clear message to the world.

title: The Fate of Vyborg
desc: The city of Vyborg was won by the Soviet Union back in 1940 when Red Army troops triumphed over the Finnish troops. Although the city was eventually retaken by Finland during the Great Patriotic War, many of our Generals believe that with [195.GetName] back in the hands of the [RUS.GetName], we should put some distance between Finland and [195.GetName] and retake what is rightfully ours.

title: [ROOT.GetNameDefCap] Retakes Vyborg!
desc: As expected, our forceds have triumped over the smaller Finnish naiton once again. As a result of this great victory, Vyborg has finally returned to our glorious Motherland. The people of [195.GetName] will rest easier now, knowly they won't have to fear an attack from the north anytime soon.

title: Finland Victorious
desc: Despite the efforts of the Army, the Finnish defence has held and routed our forces. With Vyborg firmly in Finnish hands, their government has not only demanded we relinquish our claims to the reigon but also demanded we demilitarise [195.GetName]. With much of Russia exhausted from decades of warfare, our top advisors have urged the government to accept peace and to focus on rebuilding the naiton.

title: A New Capital for the [ROOT.GetName]?
desc: Now that the Russian people have finally triumphed over Germany, it is time to decide what the future capital of Russia will be. Much of our government have supported the move to return the capital of Russia back to Moscow but there are a great deal of people who believe we should keep the capital here in [ROOT.Captial.GetName].

title: Move the Imperial Capital?
desc: With holy Russia united under our rightful flag, several members of the imperial cabinent feel that the old fortress of Chita has outlived its purpose and have proposed that we move the empire's government in another city more fit to administer the new lands, which would also provide a superior base of operations for the upcoming war with Germany. After much heated discussion and infighting amongst members of government (as well as a personal interjection from our Tsar), the issue of a new capital has been decided...

options.name: Chita shall remain the capital of the Russian Empire for the time being.
Novonikolayevsk will serve the Empire's needs.
The graves of the old Romanovs shall become the foundation of a new Empire.
Vyatka is close enough to Moscow?

title: [FROM.GetNameDefCap] Calls for [ROOT.GetAdjective] Aid!
desc:
As the war between the [GER.GetName] and the [FROM.GetName] rages in Eastern Europe, we have remained as spectators to the fighting.

Until now.

[ROOT.GetAdjective] diplomats have approached our government, requesting weapons and aid in their effort against the Reich. Whilst many in our government sympathise with the Slavs of Eastern Europe who have long endured under the German boot, there are those who fear the consequnces we would face should the Reich triumph over the Russians once more.

options.name: Offer the [FROM.GetAdjective]s our thoughts and prayers.

title: [FROM.GetNameDefCap] Agrees to Send Aid!
desc: After much consideration by the [FROM.GetAdjective] government, they have decided to support our war effort against the Wehrmacht, sending us military equipment, planes and mechanised equipment to suppliment our armies in the struggle against the [GER.GetName].

title: [FROM.GetNameDefCap] Refuses to Send Aid!
desc: Despite our best efforts by our diplomats, the [FROM.GetName] has declined to support our effort against the [GER.GetName]. Our government is highly disappointed by this result but our High Command has urged us to move on from this diplomatic set back and continue on with the liberation of Eastern Europe.

title: A Letter from Russia
desc:
Recently, we have recieved a letter from the President of the Russian Federation, requesting Italian assistance against Germany. The Russians have made a case to our government, citing the constant meddling in the Italian sphere of influence by the Reich and its puppets.

While the Russians indeed make a strong case, the question for Italy now is whether we should risk supporting Russia in their war against Germany or leave the Northern Europeans to their war effort and maintain the Mediterranian status quo.

title: Italy Agrees to Aid our Struggle
desc:
After much debate and discussion by high ranking officals within the Italian government, the Italian Empire has eagerly decided to support the Russian Federation in its effort against the German Reich.

Keen on seeing the Reich suffer the consequnces of its meddling in Mediterranian affars, Italy has provided us with financial resources and investments to help support the Russian Federation's economy and assure Russian victory against the Wehrmacht is achieved with the door for future economic and diplomatic oppertunities in the future.

options.name: Our former enemy, our newest friend.

title: Italy Refuses to Aid our Struggle
desc:
After much debate and discussion by high ranking officals within the Italian government, the Italian Empire has decided to maintain their neutrality, determining that Italy and the Mediterranian nations do not wish to endure the wrath of the Reich and the potential fallout this could cause diplomatically for the Italian government.

This response has been met with disappointment by Russia and her allies.

title: Treaty of Beijing
desc: With the negotitations now concluded, the time has come to sign the treaty of Beijing. Through peaceful means, we have achieved our goals and have retaken the occupied Far East. With the signing of the treaty, will see it's reintegration into [RUS.GetNameDef]. Millions across Russia have gathered on the streets in celebration and are eagerly waiting to welcome our Russian brothers and sisters back into the warm embrace our glorious Motherland.

title: Treaty of Beijing
desc: With the negotitations now concluded, the time has come to sign the treaty of Beijing. Through peaceful means, we have achieved most of our goals and have retaken the occupied Far East though some in our government have expressed disappointment over not being able to secure the city of Vladivostok. With the signing of the treaty, will see Outer Manchuria's reintegration into [RUS.GetNameDef]. Millions across Russia have gathered on the streets in celebration and are eagerly waiting to welcome our Russian brothers and sisters back into the warm embrace our glorious Motherland.

title: Treaty of Beijing
desc:
With the negotitations now concluded, the time has come to sign the treaty of Beijing. Through peaceful means, we have retaken the lost Birobidzhan Oblast and with the signing of the treaty, will see it's reintegration into [RUS.GetNameDef].

Although there are many in our government that are disappointed by the results, we are prepared to move ahead with the treaty and welcome our Russian brothers and sisters back into our glorious Motherland.

title: Approaching the Sphere
desc: After several weeks of chaos in Outer Manchuria and growing tension between [RUS.GetNameDef] and [JAP.GetNameDef], the Japanese have finally approached our government and has asked that we meet in the city of Beijing to discuss the future of Outer Manchuria. With the government eager to regain the occupied Far East from the Japanese, we have agreed to meet them and have sent our top diplomats to negotiate with the Japanese.

title: The Issue of Birobidzhan
desc:
The Birobidzhan Oblast has been the source of the Partisan movement in Outer Manchuria who have been battling the Japanese occupation of their homeland since their illegal annexation of the territory in the late 1940s.

The land is a majority Russian province who wish only to return to the warm embrace of their Motherland. With the return of Birobidzhan, a large chunk of the Russian partisan movement would go with it.

options.name: I'm sure they'd be happy to have it off their hands.

title: The Russians Ask for Birobidzhan
desc:
In the first round of negotiations, [RUS.GetNameDef] has requested the return of the Birobidzhan Oblast. They have argued that the province is majority Russian and is home to a large portion of the partisan movement.

Returning the land would deal with a large portion of the Russian partisan movement which is debilatating Outer Manchuria. It would be in our best interests that Russia regain its lost Oblast.

options.name: Give it back to the Russians.

title: Japan Agrees to Return Birobidzhan
desc: As many had expected, the Japanese have agreed to peacefully return the Birobidzhan Oblast, stating it would be in its best interests to do so. With the issue of Birobidzhan now concluded, we are presented with two more options. We could end the negotiations here or perhaps, we could test our luck and see if we can retake the city of Khabarvosk.

options.name: Let's not push the Japanese any further.

title: Russia Ready to Sign the Treaty
desc:
After some discussions with their government, the Russian diplomats have been given the go ahead with the signing of the Treaty.

Although we will be losing another province to the Russian state, the return of this territory will deal with the majority of our partisan problems and will benefit our Empire in the long term.

title: The Russians want Khabarovsk
desc: With the issue of Birobidzhan now resolved, the Russians are now pushing for the return of Khabarovsk and territories of Outer Manchuria. Some of our diplomats and ministers in the government have become outraged by this demand but some in our government but the Russians have grown powerful since their reunification and some in our government fear saying no to the 'Fourth Power'. The decision has ultimately fallen to the Prime Minister.

title: Japan Agrees to Return Khabarovsk
desc: After some negotiation, the Japanese have finally agreed to return Khabarovsk and Outer Manchuria to the [RUS.GetNameDef]. Our diplomats have celebrated this victory has much of what was stolen by the Japanese would now be peacefully returning to Russia where it belongs.

title: Russia Ready to Sign the Treaty
desc: With Outer Manchuria mostly back in Russian hands, [RUS.GetNameDef] is now prepared to meet with our diplomats in Beijing once more and ratify the terms that have been reached during negotiations.

title: Japan Refuses to Return Khabarovsk
desc: Despite our efforts, Japan has refused to hand over Khabarovsk and Outer Manchuria, stating that it was simply too much land to hand over to [RUS.GetNameDef]. Should we just take stock of what we have and sign the treaty or should we ask them if they we're willing to make a deal for Khabarovsk.

title: Russia wants Vladivostok Back
desc: Now that [RUS.GetNameDef] have secured much of Outer Manchuria, the Russians are now asking for the city of Urajio or Vladivostok in Russian. The Russians are really pushing it here but its an issue we should seriously consider. Should we return Vladivostok to the Russians are should we maintain our ownership of it?

options.name: Fine, they can have their precious port back.
We're gonna need some concessions from the Russians.

title: Japan Agrees to Return Vladivostok!
desc: After days of tense silence from the Japanese diplomats, the Japanese have agreed to return the city of Vladivostok back to [RUS.GetNameDef]. The news has been celebrated by our government as our nations goals in the Far East have finally been achieved.

title: The Russians are prepared to sign the treaty
desc: After weeks of negotiations, [RUS.GetNameDef], having gotten everything they wanted from Japan, are finally prepared to meet once more in Beijing and sign the treaty that would ratify the terms that have been negotiated.

options.name: For the good of the Empire.

title: Japan Proposes a Compromise
desc: Unlike Birobidzhan, Japan is not as eager to hand over Khabarovsk. They have instead proposed a deal. In exchange for handing over Khabarovsk, they have asked they maintain their resource rights in Outer Manchuria and gain access to the Tungsten reserves of the Magadan Oblast.

title: Japan Proposes a Compromise for Vladivostok
desc: After some thought, the Japanese diplomats have proposed [RUS.GetNameDef] a compromise they find reasonable. Japan is still going through an oil crisis that has handicapped their economy for some time. In exchange for the return of Vladivostok, the Japanese are asking for access to Siberian oil reserves to support their economy as well as the safe passsage of the Dongbei residents to Manchuria.

title: Japan Refuses Vladivostok
desc: Japan has refused to handover the port city of Vladivostok, stating it was an important city for the Empire and essential in maintaining their superiority in sea of Japan. They would not simply hand it over to [RUS.GetNameDef]. Should we just take stock of what we have and sign the treaty or should we ask them if they we're willing to make a deal for Vladivostok.

title: Reintegrating the Far East
desc: After years of separation, the Far East is finally ready to rejoin our Motherland. Across the Federation, the people are celebrating the return of rightfully Russian land as the President continues to fulfil his promise of liberating all Russian citizens from the oppression of tyrannical powers and reintegrating our rightful territories into the Russian Federation.

title: Russia Requests our Support
desc:
After the unification of Russia, there had been relative silence from the unified state until now. An envoy from the [RUS.GetName] has arrived in Washington concerning their attempt to negotiate with Japan for the return of the lands of Outer Manchuria. They believe that with our aid, they can put more pressure on Japan to cede the territory.

This young Russian nation has shown potential, and with our help, they might warm up more to us in the future; however, we cannot forget the other side of the talks, Japan.

As our enemy, we would love for nothing more than to weaken Japan, but the State Department doubts the Japanese are interested in giving up land. The negotiations could easily fail, and the Japanese would remember such a slight. Refusal, though, would make the Russians mad as well.

The final choice is yours, Mr. President.

options.name: Get a Russian to LA, quickly!

title: The United States Declines
desc:
Despite the best efforts of our diplomats, the Americans have declined to assist in our efforts to retake Vladivostok. Some in our foreign ministry have blamed efforts of the State Department to improve relations with the Japanese, while others point to ideological and governmental differences between our regimes. Whatever the reason, we are officially out in the cold.

Reports indicate the Japanese have taken America's noninvolvement as an endorsement of their position, an allegation which has scurried through the entire Co-Prosperity Sphere in a matter of days. Even nations sympathetic to our cause are beginning to distance themselves from this issue. If we are to retake Vladivostok, we must press down on the scales of diplomacy- and HARD.

options.name: Who cares what the Americans think, anyway?

title: The United States Accepts
desc:
Excellent news! Our plea for aid has been accepted by the United States of America. When we next enter negotiations with the Japanese, the State Department will be there to mediate- and subtly turn the negotiations to our favor. We might just have a chance at pulling this off.

Reports indicate that the Japanese have taken America's involvement as pressure to accept our claims. Of course, this is correct. Even nations closely tied to the Co-Prosperity Sphere are pressing for the Japanese to find an “honorable resolution” to the Vladivostock issue, for fear of retaliation from the OFN. While military action from the Americans is almost certainly off the table, we won't tell the Japanese. Let the specter of another Pacific Theater dance in their heads, and their imaginations will do the rest.

title: Biluobizhan Negotations
desc:
The incorrigible barbarians of [RUS.GetNameDef] have had the gall to demand the return of the region of Biluobizhan to their government. These fools believe their wretched empire, a nation which emerged from anarchy only a scant few years ago, has the right to negotiate with The Land of the Rising Sun. Worse still, the world seems to agree with them.

To save face, we must attend the negotiations, and we must do so in good faith. As the old proverb says, supply salt to your enemy. And yet, it is also said that the mouth is the source of all disasters. May it be so to these Russian ingrates.

The region of Biluobizhan is of little value to us. Overwhelmingly populated by persons of Russian ethnicity, the region is a hotbed of partisans and rebels, one we can scarcely afford to police for its vast unrest. We could simply give up the region. This would certainly be a fortuitous development in regards to our budget and to the empire's stability. Yet such an action would be extremely unpopular, especially amongst the Army. As we attempt to balance the interests of the Navy and the Army, it may not be in our interests to upset the Generals so.

But there is another option. We can bring the Russians to the negotiating table and request an exchange. Russia is rich in natural resources, especially oil and precious metals. If we were able to sell this useless scrap of land in return for the oil we so desperately need to fuel our war machine… Well, the Generals can hardly object to that, can they...

options.name: The Empire is strongest without dead weight. Give them Biluobizhan.
Pathetic. Have them try it again in a few years once they figure out how to conduct diplomacy.
Why give up the land for free, when we could profit from this indiscretion? Bring them to the negotiating table.

title: Japan Accepts!
desc:
Great news from the negotiating table! Our diplomats have won the province of Birobidzhan through hard-nosed stubbornness, a bit of compensation, and some fascinating and totally coincidental revolts by ethnic Russians in the region. We are one step closer to achieving our goals of uniting all of continental Russia.

However, we are not done with the negotiations. Our people and especially our hawkish politicians want more, along with the partisans we've recently liberated. While Birobidzhan was a hotbed of Russian insurgents, our people at home and in Outer Manchuria want us to go further, to push for Khabarovsk, all of Primorski Krai, and even Vladivostok. It will take continued careful negotiations, some strong-arming, and perhaps some foreign assistance, but we will push through to the best of our ability for our Motherland and our people.

title: Japan Walks Out!
desc:
To the leadership of [RUS.GetName],

While we are aware of the issues in administering the province of Biluobizhan, we cannot accept any offer which does not do us the minimal respect of at least compensating our government for a cession of territory. As such, we will not be able to complete the request.

Furthermore, the rancorous behavior displayed in these negotiations leads me to question the viability of future discussions. Therefore, we will be cutting off future discussions for the forseeable future.

We apologize if this is an unfortunate result for you all, as it is for us.

Signed,
Suga Nishidda, of [JAP.GetNameDef].

title: A Japanese Counteroffer
desc: The Japanese have returned to us with a counteroffer for the region of "Biluobizhan". They ask for a total payment that amounts to 800 million US dollars, which is they claim is necessary compensation for the territory they will cede to us. Some within our government question if the region is even worth that amount of money, yet others protest that any rightful territory of ours is worth more than money can buy.

title: Eyes On The Prize
desc:
After months of tense compromise, negotiations and strong-arming, the Japanese and our government have finally agreed to allow for Primorsky and Khabarovsk to return to the fold of our administration.

Our diplomats and government are surprised at the success of the negotiations. Now, we are closing in on reclaiming the last stronghold of Japanese occupation in the Far East, the city of Vladivostok. Vladivostok, unlike the natural resource-filled states that we've reclaimed, is unique. Not only does it have a significant amount of infrastructure and development, but is the sole city of Outer Manchuria which has a warm water port. It is essential for projecting our economy eastwards and strengthening our trade routes. Therefore, it is of vital importance that we try to regain the King of the East once and for all, through all diplomacy needed.

However, just as we will put everything into winning back Vladivostok, we must expect the Japanese to have an equal dedication to keeping the port themselves, knowing the problems that a Russian resurgence may pose in the Far East and their holdings in Korea and Manchuria. Even more relevant is that Russian partisans are unavailable to us, due to the displacement of Russians in the fifties to make room for “Dongbei”, or Korean, Japanese and Chinese communities.

This battle will be one of the hardest we will fight in the boardrooms and offices of the Co-Prosperity Sphere. Soon the Treaty will be signed, and the fate of Vladivostok and the Far East sealed forever. Let us persuade them with all of our intellect, skill and money, and finish with a resounding victory!

options.name: The Shining Jewel of the East is in our sights!

title: The End of Everything
desc: It is over. With our troops having recently entered Germany itself, it seems that the Führer has decided to use the nuclear option. Thousands of German nuclear missiles are already flying high in the sky, en-route to our population centers at supersonic speeds. There is nothing more to be done.

title: [Get_newspaper_header]Successful Tests of Russian Nuclear Weapons
desc:
Unexpectedly for everyone, German sailors, who have bases and access to the controlled archipelago of Novaya Zemlya, will report an unknown spike in radiation levels in the local air. Based on the analysis and wind direction, it was determined that the epicenter of the explosion was the coastal area near the Arctic Ocean - Salekhard. A few hours later, it becomes clear that the now reunited Russia has finally acquired weapons of mass destruction...

Since few in the world believed in the ability of some warlord in Russian anarchy to unite Russia, let alone research and test its own nuclear weapons in such a short time, now all of humanity is truly living for today. With the emergence of a new nuclear power on the world stage, and such an unreliable player in the form of a unified Russia, the world has once again entered a tense period of uncertainty. Germania and Tokyo have already officially condemned the successful testing of nuclear weapons, threatening to impose numerous sanctions on the new competitor if it doesn't stop the further accumulation of new strategic weapons.

options.name: Let's hope for peace to continue...

title: The Matter of Perm-on-Amur
desc:
Perm-on-Amur is a city of little value but all the more significance, situated far from Khabarovsk in Outer Manchuria. At least, that's how the Manchus see it. Renaming it to Chumin when it was annexed into their miserable puppet kingdom of Manchukuo, as they did when they stole the great eastern jewel of Vladivostok.

To Rodzaevsky, however, it represents precisely the resource that will ensure the survival of the Vozhd's state in the Far East. Therefore, it is also a place for the strengthening of the RFP and Russian National Socialism, which will significantly swell its ranks, and once we hold the entirety of Russia it will be the birthplace of the nation itself. As any good nationalist knows, having one's home occupied by foreign invaders is an unacceptable state of affairs and does severe harm to the morale of the people. Just as the Tsars would have fought tooth and nail for Saint Petersburg, we must have Perm-on-Amur!

Thankfully, since neither the Japanese nor their Manchu servants have any real interest in the city, they are unlikely to have any good reason for turning down the Vozhd's righteous claim for our sovereign territory. They will lose a 'troublesome' population, poor region and gain our eternal gratitude... with the addition of some reasonable concessions to their greedy industrialists, no doubt.

title: An Unusual Request
desc:
Our Manchurian consulate has received a rare communique from Konstantin Rodzaevsky, one of our old useful idiots from Harbin. In his capacity as 'Vozhd of the Russians', he demands in rather bipolar language the return of Nikolaevsk, a region in the far east of Manchukuo where the remote city of Chumin is located. This region has become a burden for us and our biggest administrative headache. Moreover, it is full of ethnic Russians, whom it is extremely difficult to evict due to the geographical characteristics of the area.

The Manchurians expressed their profound indifference to the matter when it was brought to their government, so there's no need to bother getting them to rubber-stamp it. All other authorities concerned have made clear that they don't care about a frozen stub of land full of troublesome Russians, and Rodzaevsky is offering us rights to the resources in far-eastern Siberia once he secures the region. Though unlikely to happen, it would allow for some interesting investment opportunities should he succeed, so there's nothing to lose from ceding the lands in question. We may as well just send the request up the pipeline to the Kantōgun and see what comes of it. We should receive a response in a few weeks or so.

options.name: I never liked that place anyway.

title: Japan Accepts Our Offer!
desc:
Joyous day! Glorious, happy day! The Japanese, ever our stalwart ally against the Reds and their servants, have agreed to cede Nikolaevsk to our All-Russian Government! It's been a little over a year since we first heard confirmation that the Kantōgun would review our request, and the wait has finally paid off. This morning, a Japanese Kantōgun officer arrived by plane to formally hand over the territory, with the Vozhd putting his signature to the agreement in his Rodzaevsk headquarters.

In return for transferring Nikolaevsk, we have granted the Japanese special rights to some of the natural resources in far-eastern Siberia. Once we secure those resources and unite the region under a stable government, the resultant trade and mining deals will no doubt prove extremely fruitful for our reborn Russian state!

For now, the Vozhd has publicly confirmed that he will travel to his newly acquired Perm-on-Amur city post-haste for a grand celebration now that it is officially back in Russian hands. Doubtless the people will be overjoyed to live under our enlightened National Socialist rule, rather than the uncaring and distant Manchus!

title: Homecoming with a Renaming
desc:
Rapturous joy filled the streets of Permskoye-na-Amure today when Rodzaevsky and his loyal protégé Okhotin arrived. The populace, encouraged by Blackshirts who handed out swastika flags and portraits of the Vozhd, turned out in their hundreds to cheer on our glorious leader's procession as they marched through the chilly morning air to the town hall. There, the mayor granted the Vozhd the keys to the city and led the crowd in a rousing rendition of 'Farewell of Slavianka'.

The Vozhd was visibly overjoyed to be back in a city of such significance to the entire region, his voice occasionally cracked as he addressed the enthralled crowd and the armed Blackshirts keeping guard. "This day will certainly go down in the history of our great nation." he stated. "Today, we have secured the the very seat of the All-Russian Government. For here I, Vozhd of the Russians, am ready to dictate my rules to the entire Russian Far East. Here, over fifty years ago, the Russia's divine destiny began to take shape! Here, Holy Russia saw the natural continuation of its rebirth! Glory to Russia!"

The Vozhd had one further honor to bestow upon this city for the loyalty of his entourage: henceforth, by Vozhd's Decree, it shall forever bear the name of his faithful right-hand man, Okhotin! Chumin is dead! Long live the loyal people of Okhotin-on-Amur!

title: Mobilization
desc: “...... The nascent central power will no longer be weak. We will destroy the Nazis in Germany, we will liberate all of Eastern Europe and restore the Motherland. "In the center of Samara, the commissar stands on a makeshift platform and speaks to the people on orders from his superiors. In addition to Russians, there are also refugees from Ukraine, Poland, and the Baltics, as well as Tatars, Kazakhs and other Central Asian nomads. The commissar could clearly feel the confusion and uneasiness of the audience, and everyone was eagerly waiting for his next sentence. n"First, we will return to Central Asia and restore order in the steppes, and then ......"n"The hegemony of ethnic Russians has long since ended, do you still want to turn Kazakhstan into a Russian colony, as Peter the Great did? A Kazakh man in the front row was agitated and scolded. The commissar was just smiling, but in fact the purpose of his trip was to unite the various ethnic groups that existed in the land of Samara against the Nazis. He turned to the makeshift map hanging on the wall behind him and calmly analyzed: "'The current Kazakhstan seems to be unified and stable, but in the south, the Turkic army supported by the German fascists is rising. The collapse of the former Soviet Union created a political vacuum in Central Asia, and the Nazis wanted to extend their claws further afield, and they have long coveted the regimes of Central Asian countries. Do you want your homeland to become a Nazi governor's palace like Poland? nThe whispers in the audience have weakened. "We will then negotiate with Japan to take back our legitimate rights and interests in Vladivostok. Our Kamchatka fleet dominates the waves, our guerrillas in Manchuria have begun to move, and Japan, which has just experienced an oil crisis, is too weak to refuse our offer. "It's all about our ultimate goal: westward expansion. The commissar pointed to the black area on the map, "Our relatives, our hometown, our comrades, who are still living under the iron heel of the Nazis." The rampant madness of German fascism today is nothing more than a foundation on our suffering, but it is a pity that the losers of the past have returned and returned with a military strength that is not what it used to be! The crowd applauded, no matter men, women and children, no matter what nationality they came from, no one was not boiling. So, a seed was planted in people's hearts:

title: Open the door to opportunity
desc:
There are so many Russians who have struggled in poverty all their lives, eager to improve their situation, but lack the resources to make it happen – there are too many. If we are to help them out of poverty, we need to develop their skills so that they can find gainful employment, otherwise they will never be able to afford the cost of training.

The solution is: the Employment Task Force, a new program run by the National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC) that aims to provide free vocational training to young low-income people to improve their quality of life by equipping them with the skills they need to improve their socioeconomic status.

With the advent of the Employment Task Force, we will be able to show millions of poor people in Russia a path out of the darkness of poverty, and if they are willing to move forward, they can meet a bright future ahead.

title: A day in the life of the Minister of Economy
desc:
[RUS.GetName] Minister of Economy was in his office as usual to revise the papers, and as a mountain of papers was handed out as executive orders, the last work of the morning was quickly presented - this was drafted by the General Secretary himself, representing the great importance he attaches to Russia's economic policy: "Our General Principles of the Economy" He narrowed his eyes and carefully studied his frowning brow gradually unfolded, and then at the end of the document [RUS.GetLeader] signed his name in front of him, and he breathed a sigh of relief and enjoyed his rare leisure time.
……
In the cafeteria, the minister took out a large bottle of Coke with a smile on his face, and with the relaxing sound of carbonated bubbles, he said to his colleagues: "Comrades, I announce to you that our work has been successfully completed in stages, and ...... We can go back to our normal vacation!" Suddenly, cheers abounded, and even the most serious old Artyom's face showed a knowing smile.
After the meal, the Minister of Economy strolled through the streets and looked at the commercial street ahead that was being rebuilt after the demolition of dilapidated buildings in accordance with the city plan. Half a month ago, it was just a flat vacant lot, but now the frame of the building has risen from the ground. Their emerging country, like this street, is thriving, albeit in ruins. He thought: "Truckloads of reinforced concrete are sent to the construction site, turning into the bones and flesh of the city, and those who work hard for the city...

options.name: They are the soul of the city. ”

title: Pre-assessment
desc:
We did it.
Since the fall of the Russian land under the iron heel of the Nazis, the fragmentation of her land, and the fratricidal killing of her children, many people have come to believe that there is no possibility of reunification in Russia. Now, however, we have unified most of Russia, and most of the fragments of the alliance have been recovered by us, and everything seems to be moving in a good direction.
"To be honest, although our strength is now comparable to the vast majority of countries in the world." The foreign minister scrutinized each sentence as much as he could, trying to make the rest of the sentence seem less heavy. "But as far as the restoration of the Soviet Union is concerned... With our current strength....it is indeed very difficult. ”
[RUS.GetLeader] frowned:“Such of?”
"By the time we were recovering Russia and purging the traitors and Nazis, the outside world had changed dramatically. Our old adversary, Nazi Germany, had survived the oil crisis, and although they were hit hard in this crisis, their military strength had also increased dramatically during the period of our unification of Russia, and their collaborators were all over Eurasia, so to speak, our enemies were still a suffocating force across continents. ”
"In addition, our Japan in the East should not be underestimated." After the Minister of Foreign Affairs had finished speaking, the Minister of Intelligence continued. "After the unification of Russia, they have increased their presence in the East, which has created a new round of threats to our Far Eastern territories. And a new round of encirclement and suppression has been carried out against our compatriots in the Far East, and with our current national strength, we cannot withstand a two-front battle. ”
"Moreover, many of our neighbours, as well as many of our former republics, have not welcomed our reunification, fearing that our return will result in the loss of their independence, and that some areas have even been taken over by the Nazis. threatens our security. ”
[RUS.GetLeader] listened to these returns, and his thoughts drifted back home. Although Russia is unified, there are many domestic governance affairs. Although the coalition destroyed the different forms of political power established during the period of secession, it was not so easy to eliminate the remnants of these forces from all sides at the grassroots level. The newly liberated land was full of ruins, the people were hungry and cold, and the country's production capacity could not even catch up with that before the Soviet-German war. Although the entire leadership had prepared for the worst for the liberation of the country, when it came time to actually assess it, the plan was far from catching up with the changes.
"Listen, guys." [RUS.GetLeader] looked at each of the ministers in attendance. "Our work plan will be changed, the recovery of occupied areas such as Moscow will no longer be carried out immediately, we will need some time to recover and develop, to rebuild our country." He turned to the Minister of Foreign Affairs. "In the meantime, we also need to reconcile with the United States, enlist the support of more powers in the world, and expand our influence"
"In any case, we have united the whole country under one banner, and as long as we do it well, then I believe that in less than a few years, we will be able to fight back to Moscow and make the Nazis pay for it with blood!"

options.name: One day, the red flag will come to Moscow again.

title: Iron and sweat
desc:
The train pulls into Kuibyshev, and the window is full of ruins and broken bridges. [ROOT.GetLeader] Standing on the platform, swept his gaze over the workers and displaced people cleaning up the rubble, and whispered: n"This is not the city we want. We will not mend the past, we will build a new future. ”
- The "Urban Development Plan of the USSR" came into being.
"We're not going to rebuild the old towns, we're going to demolish them." At Rykov's city planning conference, the old buildings were crossed out of the blueprints with a red pen and replaced by cultural palaces and collective apartments. The general secretary pointed to the center of the map: "Here, the largest workers' square in Western Russia will be built." ”  
"We're not going to rebuild the old towns, we're going to demolish them." At Rykov's city planning conference, the old buildings were crossed out of the blueprints with a red pen and replaced by cultural palaces and collective apartments. The general secretary pointed to the center of the map: "Here, the largest workers' square in Western Russia will be built." "A new city will rise from the ruins."
A pilot project in a workers' residential complex in the city of Gorky was launched. Central heating, public bathhouse, free nursery, canteen
For the first time, a working family has a home of their own.
"Is this really for us to live in?" Standing in front of the door of the new apartment, Vasily asked, stunned for a while.
The distribution officer smiled and patted him on the shoulder: "Of course, this is your home. ”  
"This is the first time the city has truly belonged to us."
The factory area in Irkutsk was launched, with direct access to the workshop by subway, and workers could reach their jobs in 20 minutes on foot.
The industrial park in Kazan has not only production workshops, but also canteens, clinics, cinemas, sports grounds, where workers are no longer vassals of machines, but masters of life.
"A factory is not just a place for production, it is a fortress and home for workers."
But the road to construction was not smooth.
"We lack cement, steel, electricity." The handwriting of the report is messy. The government immediately issued an "All-Russian Labor Mobilization Order", and millions of workers, peasants, and demobilized soldiers flocked to the construction site, working day and night.
In Sverdlov, young engineers worked all night designing heating systems; On the banks of the Volga, workers braved the cold wind to build bridges. Everyone knows that they are part of a project that will shape the future.
The first new cities sprung up.
Early in the morning, the workers walked out of their apartments and walked to the factory; The mother pushes the stroller and crosses the boulevard towards the free nursery. Songs of victory were broadcast on the radio, and reports of success were posted on the streets.
On Rykov's Central Square, a red banner was unfurled in the wind:  
"The workers created the city, and the city will belong to the workers!"
[ROOT.GetLeader] sat at his desk and looked at the first city of the new world, his eyes like a torch.

options.name: Even if it's a long road.

title: Sow the seeds of knowledge
desc:
As the morning sun fell on an elementary school on the outskirts of Rykov, the blackboard was written in chalk with the theme of today's lesson: "The Victory of the Soviets and the Future of the People." Grigory Ivanovich, an elderly teacher, stood on the podium, tapped lightly on the blackboard, and looked into the immature but eager eyes of the classroom. He cleared his throat and said slowly: "Children, you are the future of the new Russia, you no longer have to endure war and hunger, we will pave a bright path for you." ”
His voice echoed through the classroom, while outside the window, hordes of workers and the Red Army were rebuilding the devastated land. The flames of revolution once swept across the land, and the decay of the old world was completely swept away, but the construction of the new world was far more difficult than the destruction.
The Central People's Commissariat of Education recently promulgated a far-reaching bill - the All-Russian Law on the Reform of Compulsory Education. At the heart of the bill is the idea that every child, whether they are workers, peasants, or former bourgeoisie, should have access to a complete education.

options.name: Knowledge is a traveling companion on any path.

title: New Social Security Law
desc:
The night was still cold, but the lights of the Supreme Soviet remained unextinguished throughout the night. The hours-long meeting was still going on, and the smell of burnt cigarettes and the rustle of paper were in the air. Members of the Supreme Soviet sat around the conference table, wearily flipping through the documents before them, discussing an issue that would concern the lives and deaths of millions of Russians — the All-Russian Social Security Programme.
"We won the war." A commissioner in a gray military uniform said tiredly, rubbing his bloodshot eyes, "But what about our people? They have nothing left. ”
The victory of the revolution does not mean the end of suffering. Mother Russia is moaning, and the Russian people are still struggling to survive. The war had destroyed factories, fields and railways, millions of orphans had lost loved ones roaming the streets, the disabled Red Army had endured hunger and cold in dilapidated houses, and elderly mothers wept over the bones of their children. The revolution promised a better future, and now, the future must deliver on its promises.
This newly adopted social security programme will be the first cornerstone of the new Soviet state.

The implementation of the new programme has not been without cost.
"These projects require more money than we can afford!" The Minister of Finance spread out the ledger at the meeting, his voice trembling with anger, "We have just finished the revolution and the treasury is empty!" If we increase the financial burden, our economy will collapse."
After listening in silence,[RUS.GetLeader] reached out and picked up a report on the factory's increase in production capacity, and gently placed it on the table: "We have the toughest workers, we have the bravest Red Army, and they can rebuild the country – but only if they survive." ”
Eventually, the plan was adopted. In order to prop up the social security system, the government announced nationwide labor mobilization, factories worked overtime, kulak property was expropriated, and the wartime emergency economic system was maintained. But at the same time, new housing, new factories, and new schools are springing up all over the country.
When the first workers, mothers, veterans, and orphans received their own allowances, they knew that this was not a bourgeois handout, but a victory for themselves.
At night, the Kremlin lights finally went out, and in the streets, workers gathered in front of a new bulletin that had just been posted, silently reading its headline:
New All-Russian Social Security Programme

options.name: - For the people, not just for the revolution.

title: Expand the army
desc:
Barracks for a day,
Kuibyshev, where a certain company was stationed.
A new batch of young men answered the call of the alliance to join the army.
"I am! Captain Vasily! I'm here to train you! We, veterans of the Western Russian War, are the best of you! Big brother! If you have anything you don't understand, you can ask us, and we will tell you kindly! Now, please introduce yourself! Each person brings their own name and introduction! Start with you! ”
"Yes! Rykov, George M.I..."
"I want to the Nazi scum so quietly! Do it all over again! ”
"Yes! Rykov City! Georgy Mikhailov! ”
"Good! Next"
"Gorky! Moisei Petrov! ”
"Good! Very energetic! Next! ”
"Vologda, Nikolai Ivanovich."
"I can't hear clearly! Can't hear at all! It's too quiet! There is no Union military look! Do it all over again! ”
"What?! Didn't you hear?! ”
"Don't look away! Don't look around! Are you in an upright position?! ”
"In the barracks, the company command said that it could not be heard, that is, it could not be heard! Do it all over again! ”

title: No Time to Waste
desc:
In the Ministry of Finance office in the capital, stacks of unusually tall financial reports caught the Minister of Economy's attention. Unlike usual, these reports, without exception, concerned local financial difficulties due to tax resistance:
In Nizhny Tagil, workers seized control of the arms factory, demanding an 'end to their exploitation through taxes'; in Barnaul, angry peasants used farm tools to drive away officials who came to collect grain taxes; in Magadan, merchants engaged in overseas trade formed a joint chamber of commerce, threatening the government to lower business taxes, or else they would resort to strikes and market closures.
Though mentally prepared, these reports still threw Volpin and his team into a flurry of activity. As an economist, he was well aware of the deep-seated economic ailments of his homeland. The originally long-term, moderate reform plan was now precarious due to this crisis. But if a decisive and thorough tax reform was not carried out now, the nation's financial situation would face an unprecedented crisis.
Indeed, he also knew that any reform would touch upon someone's interests, and voices of opposition would only increase. Thus, Volpin found himself in a dilemma: on one hand, the myriad citizens of the motherland had long suffered under burdensome tax policies, and rashly reducing their taxes might lead to the collapse of the financial system; on the other hand, the high-income groups in the country would undoubtedly try every means to resist paying taxes, and rashly increasing their taxes would certainly invite their counterattacks and retaliation...
Time ticked by, second by second. Volpin could no longer hear the commotion in the office. His gaze fell upon the uneven and teetering scales on his desk. [RUS.GetName]'s financial system was slowing towards the abyss of collapse. He had to...
And immediately, he made his final decision:

options.name: We should skim some fat off them.

title: The Sin of Greed
desc:
Mr. Barannikov sat limply in the defendant's dock, his brow furrowed, a hint of unease in his eyes. The atmosphere in the courtroom was tense and solemn; the gazes of the judge and jury were all focused on him. Unlike usual, he wasn't wearing his dark suit; due to his hasty journey, he only had time to put on a shirt. He didn't look as vibrant as he usually did on television and in newspapers; his eyes were full of exhaustion.
“Court is now in session…”
Now, his palms were slightly sweaty from nervousness. The lawyer he had hired at great expense stood beside him, his voice firm and powerful, defending him. Barannikov listened to the lawyer's statement, feeling anxious. His Gaikin Group had supplied [RUS.GetName] with countless armaments, and of course, he had amassed immeasurable wealth. However, the implementation of the new tax policy was attempting to make him surrender his wealth, but for him, a man誰 money, this was absolutely impossible.
“The defendant, Gaikin Group, by exploiting multiple tax loopholes…”
He began to seek various methods to evade it all. For this, he hired the best tax consultants, attempting to protect his assets. But no matter what, all efforts seemed futile—in the end, he still found himself in the defendant's dock.
“Mr. Barannikov…”
The judge's questions were sharp and direct. Barannikov hesitated somewhat in his answers. His voice was low, occasionally stuttering due to nervousness. He had to avoid the judge's sharp gaze to find some inner peace.
Outside the court, reporters gathered at the entrance, their camera flashes constantly flickering, trying to uncover all the details of this case that could arguably decide the future of the Republic. Inside, the spectators were also whispering, exchanging their views. As the trial proceeded, his mood grew heavier. He knew the chances of winning this silent war against the tax bureau were slim. A flicker of hesitation crossed his eyes, but it was quickly replaced by a determined expression. He still hoped, no, he *had* to find a glimmer of hope, absolutely could not let these scoundrels touch his property, absolutely not…
“Silence!”
Evidence continued to be presented, his hopes gradually shattering, his sanity slowly eroding—his property, his everything. From the expressions of the judge and jury, he knew it was irreparable. Barannikov's mood shifted from nervousness to despair, followed by endless rage. He could bear it no longer, stood up and shouted, like a monkey performing an impromptu act:
“I’ve done so damn much for this country, damn it, how dare you treat me like this?!”
“The defendant will remain silent! Please observe court discipline.”
The bailiff pressed him back into his seat. No one paid him any attention; everyone tensely awaited the final result:
“It’s all over…”
They covered their faces and wept, crying out loud. The snowflakes they had created in the old era now roared and charged at them. The last shred of hope was extinguished with the judge's verdict.
“The sentence is hereby pronounced…”
“The court upholds the decision of the tax bureau. After the establishment of the Gaikin Group, Barannikov, through tax loopholes, allowed the Gaikin Group to evade billions in taxes, causing immeasurable losses to [RUS.GetName] and society. Therefore, the Gaikin Group must pay back taxes of approximately 1.3 billion rubles and a fine of approximately 700 million rubles, all to be paid in full within six months…”

options.name: They could only accept this outcome grimly.

title: After the Dark Night...
desc:
Before the tax cuts, Andrei's life was full of hardship. Every day, he toiled in the coal mine, sweat soaking his work clothes. His face always wore a look of fatigue, his eyes revealing a helplessness towards life. His wages barely maintained his family's basic living, and the heavy tax burden made him feel suffocated.
“How come the tax has gone up again?” Andrei complained at dinner, a hint of anxiety in his voice. His wife, Maria, listened silently, a worried look on her face. Their child, little Ivan, looked at them curiously, not understanding why his parents were always troubled by money. Andrei's brow was tightly furrowed, his eyes filled with worry about the future.
Their meals were always simple; an occasional piece of meat was a luxury. Andrei's shoes were long worn out, but he couldn't bear to buy new ones. Maria's clothes were always the same few, washed anúncios. Though life was simple, the high taxes always hung over their hearts, constantly extinguishing any warmth, suffocating them.
Later, Andrei decided to join the tax resistance protests, hoping to change the situation through collective strength. On the day of the protest, he stood among the crowd, holding a banner, shouting slogans loudly. His eyes were determined, his voice full of hope.
“We can't live like this anymore!” Andrei shouted, his voice echoing through the crowd. The loud voices spread like waves through the crowd, superimposing, eventually permeating the streets and alleys of Krasnoyarsk. At that moment, he felt an unprecedented strength, as if his voice could change the world. He felt his body filled with vitality, his heartbeat rising and falling with the waves. He felt he was no longer an ordinary coal miner, but a warrior fighting for justice and the future.
After several tax resistance protests, the government finally decided to implement tax cuts for ordinary people. The day the news arrived, Andrei was working in the coal mine. When he heard the news, he could hardly believe his ears.
“Really? Are the taxes really going down?” he asked his colleague excitedly, tears welling in his eyes. His voice trembled, but it was full of joy. His colleagues also responded excitedly; this was the fruit of their victory.
Now, Andrei's life has undergone a tremendous change. He no longer needs to work overtime to pay taxes, and life is no longer as constrained as before due to high taxes. The improvement in quality of life also allows him more time and energy to spend with his family.
“Look, Maria, we can finally buy Ivan the toy he’s always wanted,” Andrei said excitedly, holding his newly received wages, his voice full of happiness. Maria smiled at him, tears also welling in her eyes.
On the first weekend after the tax cuts, Andrei's family went for a picnic in the park early in the morning. Watching Ivan run on the grass, a long-lost smile reappeared on the couple's faces.
“Dad, look, I caught a butterfly!” Ivan ran over excitedly, holding a colorful butterfly in his hand. Andrei and Maria looked at him, this little fellow filling their hearts with pride and happiness. Their smiles were so radiant, so sincere, as if all their troubles had vanished into thin air.
Countless families like Andrei's were also enjoying this hard-earned leisure. The morning sunlight shone on their faces. Life, though not as beautiful as they had imagined, would never again be as laborious and tiring as before.

title: The Storm Abates, For Now
desc:
Inside the office, the lights were dim, only the faint glow from computer screens illuminated the room. To get [RUS.GetName]'s finances back on track as soon as possible, the Minister of Economy and his team had been working continuously for weeks. Everyone looked exhausted, but no one dared to slacken their efforts in the slightest.
The tables were piled high with documents and coffee cups. A map of Russia hung on the wall, with financially distressed regions marked in red. Outside, the night view of Moscow appeared exceptionally tranquil in the darkness. Pedestrians walked by rustling softly, completely unaware of the intense work underway in the nearby office.
Long nights had left dark circles under the Minister's eyes. Though weary, his gaze remained firm. He understood that if they did not fight these difficulties to the death, only endless depression awaited the motherland.
“Minister!” A startled cry suddenly rang out in the office. “Magadan’s report has finally been submitted! Their financial system can finally operate normally this month.”
“We did it,” the Minister’s voice was hoarse, but joy was still evident. “Our reform measures are starting to take effect.”
He felt an unprecedented sense of accomplishment, but soon, a deep weariness washed over him again. He knew this was just the beginning; they still had a long way to go. Cheers erupted in the office; they knew what this report meant.
The Minister crossed off the last red circle on the map. Looking at the densely crossed-out red circles, thinking of how those wealthy merchants and dignitaries had finally shut their mouths, he now had enough funds for the next step of reform.
“Have Magadan and other places recompile new financial reports and send them over. We need more precise data to guide our decisions,” the Minister emphasized. “We must ensure our reforms not only solve current problems but also lay a solid foundation for future development.”
“We cannot stop here,” the Minister murmured. “The foundations of tax reform are still not solid enough. We need to keep moving forward, until we achieve final victory.”
After a moment of silence, the Minister took out the tax reform plan that had been idle for some time. Although it had once been nearly scrapped due to this crisis, after much mending and patching, it was now ready to be reactivated.
“Get [RUS.GetLeader] on the phone,” the Minister said. “Now we have to roll up our sleeves and give this country a resounding revolution.”

options.name: Everyone, back to your posts. We still have much to do.

title: [RUS.GetName] Tax Reduction Act
desc:

1. Goals:

Promote consumption and stimulate economic growth.
Enhance the fairness and transparency of the tax system.

Transparency: Simplify tax laws and improve the transparency of tax policies.

title: The River of Funds Flows On...
desc:
Syktyvkar, during the years of the Komi Republic, was filled with violence, conspiracy, and madness. But now, it bathes in the morning sun. On the streets, people are burying the traces of Pandora's Box in the ruins of the past. As funds from [RUS.GetName] begin to flow into this war-torn city, people are dismantling the ubiquitous armories and fortifications along the streets, hope and determination re-emerging on their faces. In the future, Syktyvkar may not become Russia's most beautiful or prosperous city, but it will certainly not be like the city of the past.
Omsk was almost entirely destroyed during the war, but it is now undergoing tremendous changes. Investment from [RUS.GetName] has not only greatly improved the city's appearance but also brought new industrial projects. The intense desire for revenge that once permeated the city is gradually fading. Thick black smoke once again billows from factory chimneys, and the roar of machinery proclaims the city's future to the heavens. Omsk's industrial heart is beating again, but unlike before, it no longer produces only guns and weapons for slaughter, but also rye bread to benefit the masses.
Tomsk, long neglected, is now ushering in its spring. Investment from [RUS.GetName] has allowed the city's cultural potential to be fully realized. In the city center, new buildings are rising one after another. Workers, free from tax burdens, labor diligently on construction sites. The roar of machinery intertwines with people's laughter, forming a harmonious symphony. Along the streets, newly planted trees are beginning to sprout tender green leaves, allowing this gray city to regain its true colors. Museums, libraries, and art centers, long unmaintained, have been revitalized, attracting tourists and scholars from all over the country. Though traces of the Central Siberian Republic are hard to find, Tomsk's cultural light is beginning to illuminate all of Russia.
Petropavlovsk, a port city once overlooked due to its remote location and the departure of the Red Navy, has now finally caught the attention of the [RUS.GetName] government, which intends to develop it into Russia's new trade center and important naval port after Magadan. Large sums of money have repaired the facilities of the abandoned port, attracting ships and merchants from all over the world. On the port's docks, goods from the OFN, and even Japan and Germany, are piled high, with merchants busily trading. Not far away, the Pacific Fleet at the Petropavlovsk naval base is conducting exercises in full swing, preparing thoroughly for future contingencies. Perhaps people should believe that this once almost desolate city does not belong to pristine nature.

title: Banners on the Dnieper
desc:
The air in Kyiv was thick with dust, smoke, and a peculiar silence—the silence that falls when artillery has just ceased, and the living dare not yet speak loudly. Ivan leaned against the shell-pocked wreck of a BTR, wearily watching the grey sky. They had done it. From the frozen north, they had pushed south, across battlefields strewn with corpses, and now the banner representing a unified Russia finally flew over this ancient city. The radio repeatedly broadcast news of victory, proclaiming that the Ukrainian people had been liberated from 'forty years of brutal fascist bandit rule' and returned to the 'embrace of the great Slavic family.'

Sounded grandiose, Ivan thought. Just like something those political department types, who’d never smelled gunpowder, would write. But what he saw before him was far removed from the radio’s fervent paeans. No welcoming crowds with food and drink, no cheering throngs. Only faces, sallow and hollow-eyed, cautiously peering out from basements and crevices in the ruins. No joy on their faces, more like numbness, doubt, and a weariness that cut to the bone. They eyed Ivan and his comrades as they would a pack of bears that had just driven off wolves but might themselves be devourer.

Yesterday, Ivan’s squad, while clearing remnants of the enemy in a half-demolished apartment building, had found an old woman hiding in a closet. She clutched a faded, strangely embroidered cloth bundle, muttering to herself in a language he almost couldn't understand, yet found vaguely familiar. Not German, not Russian. When the soldiers tried to pull her out, she fast raised her head, a nearly extinguished spark in her cloudy eyes, and said in a hoarse but startlingly clear voice: “We are Ukrainians.”

Just that one sentence. No thanks, no accusations, just a statement so simple it was almost stubborn. As if reminding them, and herself, that after the oppression of Germanization, the endless grain requisitions, the terror of the secret police, and the daily humiliations, some things, like tenacious grassroots under the black earth, had not died. Ivan had later seen hand-drawn trident symbols hidden in wall cracks in cleared houses, heard fragments of sad, off-key songs drifting from some window at night, their melodies definitely not from Moscow.

They had been ruled for forty years. Forty years, long enough for a generation to be born, grow up, and grow old. Their cities were renamed, their language forbidden in official use, their history altered or erased. Children were forced to learn German, singing songs praising another “Führer.” Wheat from the black earth was ceaselessly shipped to Germania, while locals often struggled on the brink of starvation. Ivan recalled reading about the “Holodomor” in history books, a tragedy of another era, but for many elderly people here, perhaps it was just a repetition in a different form.

Now, they were “liberated.” Tanks rolled over squares once adorned with swastikas; new portraits replaced old ones. But looking at those silent, complex-eyed Ukrainians, Ivan suddenly felt a wave of confusion. How should history be remembered? Whose sacrifices should be eulogized? Whose suffering should be recounted? The memories carried by this land were far heavier, far more complex, than they had initially imagined. They had brought back the banner, but could they truly bring back those souls suppressed, distorted, and whispered about in the long, dark night?

Ivan sighed and re-shouldered his rifle. At least, the fighting was over. At least, they had come.

options.name: Forty years whispering a name, even iron hooves could not crush.

title: The First Brick on the Ruins
desc:
The morning mist had not yet dispersed, and sunlight struggled to penetrate the dust lingering over Kyiv, falling on the pitted cobblestones of Saint Andrew's Descent. The air was a mixture of damp earth, lime, and an indescribable scent of new beginnings. Once, this place echoed with the rhythmic tread of marching boots, sharp German commands, and occasional gunshots. Now, a different kind of symphony had taken its place—the clang of hammers striking stone, the rough chants of porters, the creak of temporary scaffolding, and... the whisper of hope.

“Comrades, put your backs into it! This wall must be finished before nightfall!” shouted a foreman wearing an old, mortar-stained military cap, his voice booming. Beneath his feet lay a scene of devastation—collapsed walls, charred beams, scattered rubble. Just a few months ago, this was a battlefield. Now, it was a construction site. Men, mostly elderly veterans or young men who had just laid down their rifles, labored in silence and with focus. They passed bricks, mixed mortar, their movements clumsy yet imbued with an almost stubborn determination. Each brick laid seemed to declare to the dark past: We are back, and we will reclaim our home.

Not far away, several women were painstakingly clearing debris with wicker baskets, their headscarves covering half their faces, revealing only eyes that were weary yet resilient. As they cleared, they spoke in low voices, an occasional suppressed sob heard, but more often, whispers of mutual encouragement. “Soon, Alyona, a few more baskets and we’ll see the foundation.” “Careful, Tamara, that stone isn’t stable.” They were clearing not just rubble, but the fragments of life buried by war—broken pottery, charred picture frames, rusted farm tools... Each item silently told a story forcibly interrupted.

Occasionally, Russian soldiers in uniform would patrol by, their gazes sweeping over the busy crowd, their expressions complex. Some would stop, awkwardly helping to move a few bricks, earning a few heavily accented “thank yous.” Others merely watched in silence, as if contemplating the meaning of this reconstruction and their role in this land. The air was no longer filled with hostility, but with a cautious coexistence, a fragile understanding built upon common ruins.

In the distance, the Dnieper River flowed silently on, reflecting the gradually brightening sky and the city’s battered skyline. The road to reconstruction was long, and the painful memories were far from healed. But this first brick, this first chant, this first ray of sunlight piercing the dust, was like a seed falling upon the traumatized black earth. Perhaps, as their poet wrote…

options.name: “When the sleeper awakens, he shall find his fetters broken.”

title: Seeds Beneath the Black Earth
desc:
Petro's boots sank deep into the muddy black earth, each step making a dull squelch. The air mixed the dampness of the early spring thaw with an indescribable smell of rusted metal and decaying bones. Was this the granary they promised? This fabled land where a walking stick planted would supposedly sprout? He looked around; the fields were pockmarked with craters, like a face ravaged by smallpox. On the distant horizon, the twisted silhouette of a derelict tank stabbed at the leaden sky, a monument left from the last liberation, or perhaps the one before that? Who could even remember.

Instructors from the city, in their clean uniforms, generously distributed seeds—small, shriveled grains in sacks الناس by faded, illegible Cyrillic letters. They patted Petro's shoulder, speaking passionately about 'Five-Year Plans,' 'agricultural modernization,' and 'contributing grain to the great motherland.' Petro just nodded, forcing a look of requisite gratitude and enthusiasm. He didn't tell the instructor that last autumn, in this very field, he had dug up an unexploded German aerial bomb that nearly sent his whole family to meet Hrut. Nor did he mention that the previous rulers had also promised tractors, only to deliver a pile of rusty parts and an incomprehensible German manual.

Neighbor Ivan squatted at the edge of the field, rolling a cheap makhorka cigarette, watching Petro struggle with his ancestral, endlessly repaired wooden plow. “Petro,” Ivan exhaled a thick cloud of smoke, his voice like sandpaper, “they say this black earth has a spirit; it knows what you plant. Do you think it knows whether we’re planting hope now, or another crop of suffering?”

Petro stopped, wiped the sweat from his brow, a mixture of soil and perspiration. “Who knows, Ivan,” he panted, “Maybe it only knows hunger. It’s been hungry for decades, and we’ve been hungry for decades. Now, someone says let us feed it, and then it will feed us. Sounds… fair.” His tone carried an almost numb sense of fatalism. Fair? On this land, 'fair' was a luxury.

He bent down, grabbed a handful of seeds from the cloth bag, the shriveled grains pricking his calloused palm. He looked at this land,hit countless times, a land that had devoured corpses, drunk blood, and borne too many broken promises. Unified. Yes, no more men in different uniforms shooting at each other here. That was progress, undoubtedly. Life was perhaps a little better, like the air by a winter fire, slightly warmer. But this land… it was so tired.

Petro took a deep breath and scattered the seeds onto the turned earth. Black grains fell on black soil, silently. Would they sprout? Would they bear fruit? Or would they be washed away by the coming rains, or pecked clean by crows? No one knew. But he scattered the seeds anyway, because what else could he do? This was his land, no matter how much pain it carried.

title: Signed, Sealed, Can't Read It
desc:
Summer had barely settled in when a new face appeared in the village—a young man with thick glasses and a neat but slightly countrified uniform, calling himself a 'Land Relations Coordinator' sent from the district. He brought several stacks of brand-new documents reeking of ink, and an enthusiasm that sent a chill down Petro's spine. The coordinator gathered the villagers in front of the dilapidated village office, gushing about the new 'land to the tiller' policy, words hailing down on Petro's muddled head like hailstones: 'cadastral registration,' 'land use certificates,' 'collective responsibility linked to individual profit'...
Petro was handed a stiff piece of paper, covered in dense Cyrillic script, and a bright red stamp depicting what looked like some kind of fierce bird. He looked at it sideways, then upright, brought it close to his eyes, then held it up to the sunlight, squinting. The letters danced before him like a swarm of drunken ants, performing an incomprehensible ballet. His rough fingers traced the paper's edge. This thing was thicker than a ration coupon, but far less substantial than a good scythe.
“Petro Ivanovich!” The young coordinator clapped him on the shoulder, his smile as bright as the red star on Moscow's square. “Congratulations! Look! This piece of land, from now on, it belongs to you! Well, strictly speaking, it’s a long-term stable use right, but practically, it’s yours! Work hard for the great motherland!”
“Mine?” Petro repeated numbly, his voice sounding like it came from a dry well. “What d’you mean? This land… hasn’t it always been me farming it? My pa farmed it, my grandpappy too. It was this piece when the Germans came, and this piece when the last liberators came. How’s it become mine now?” He pointed to the familiar patch of black earth nearby, just starting to show some green shoots. “Does this stamp on this paper make the stones in the field run away by themselves? Or will next year’s rain listen to my commands?”
Old Ivan, puffing on his pipe nearby, muttered, “Careful, Petro. The Tsar used to say the land was his, then the commissar said the land was collective, now they say the land is yours. This land, eh, it’s like a disobedient wife. Nobody’s word counts, only God Almighty’s and your own strength.”
Petro ignored Ivan's grumbling. He looked down at the 'certificate' again, trying to find some familiar trace in those twisted symbols—perhaps 'potato'? Or 'tax'? Nothing. He only recognized his own name, Petro Ivanovich, clumsily printed at the top. He suddenly felt a dizzying sense of absurdity. This land, soaked with the sweat, and occasionally the blood, of generations of his family, was now 'his' because of a piece of paper he couldn't read?
He looked up at the black field, the early summer wind carrying the scent of earth and grass. The land was still the same land, silent and stoic. Slowly, carefully, he folded the stiff paper and tucked it into the worn pocket of his shirt, right next to his heart. There, the paper's edges pressed against his skin through the coarse cloth. An unprecedented emotion, a mixture of immense confusion and a tiny, almost negligible… perhaps… hope? stirred in his numb heart like a newly sprouted seedling.
Wow… he really had land? Even if only a piece of paper he couldn't make heads or tails of said so.

options.name: Well, now this mud finally has my name on it.

title: The New 'Cooperative' Neighbors
desc:
The 'land certificate' had barely warmed in Petro's breast pocket when new developments arrived in the village. This time, it wasn't an enthusiastic young man, but a stern-faced, middle-aged man who spoke with a thick bureaucratic accent. His uniform collar was stiffer than the most presentable tablecloth in Petro's house. He summoned all the villagers who had received 'certificates' and announced a grand initiative called the 'Agricultural Production Cooperative Pilot Program.'
“Comrades!” His voice echoed in the empty village hall, carrying an undeniable authority. “Individual farming is inefficient and cannot bear the heavy responsibility of revitalizing the motherland's granary! To increase output, share resources, and concentrate efforts on major tasks, we have decided to establish agricultural cooperatives! Everyone's land, tools, and even that lame old horse,” he pointed to old Ivan's animal tied to a tree, “will be uniformly managed by the cooperative, with distribution according to labor, more work means more reward!”
Petro stood in the crowd, scratching his scalp vigorously, trying to make sense of the tongue-twisting words. Uniform management? Distribution according to labor? This sounded… awfully familiar. He remembered as a child, another group of men in different uniforms had said similar things, only then it was called a 'collective farm.' Then too, they talked about 'concentrating efforts.' And the result? The grain was indeed concentrated, but it all ended up on the grain requisition teams' trucks.
“What?” Old Ivan was the first to jump up, his pipe almost falling to the ground. “My old horse may be lame, but it's mine! Why should it be uniformly managed by you? I ask you, if I want to leave a couple of potatoes for my grandson, do I have to submit a report?”
The middle-aged official pushed up his glasses, his face impassive. “Comrade Ivan Stepanovich, this is for the common good. The cooperative will uniformly provide seeds, fertilizer, and coordinate plowing times. At the end ofthe year, income will be calculated based on work points, ensuring fairness and justice, and you'll also get priority access to state-supplied agricultural machinery.” He paused, his tone becoming more emphatic. “Of course, we won't force comrades who are unwilling to join. It's just that… farmers outside the cooperative, in terms of resource allocation and agricultural product procurement prices, may… experience some differences.”
A murmur of discussion rippled through the crowd. Petro looked at the land certificate in his hand, then at the patch of land that had just started to show some life, his mind a tangled mess. The 'his' land he had just received, barely warmed, was now to be 'cooperated'? Wasn't this just going back in a circle?
But then he thought, life had indeed gotten a bit better recently. The rationed flour, though unpalatable, was at least enough; the village road had been repaired, still a dirt road, but with fewer potholes; most importantly, he could sleep soundly at night. That young coordinator had even helped his son, little Vasya, get into primary school in the city…
Petro scratched his head again. He still couldn't understand the convoluted ways of these city folk. Collective farm? Cooperative? It sounded like the big bad wolf in a new disguise. But… his stomach did feel a bit fuller than before. He sighed heavily and, like the other villagers, pressed his fingerprint onto another document he couldn't understand.

options.name: Alright, a different way to play in the mud together.

title: Divided Land, Familiar Taste
desc:
Mikhail, shouldering his oft-repaired old plow, trudged through the tilled black earth. The scent of spring finally overpowered the muddy odor of melting snow, carrying a faint, elusive fragrance of grass. Unlike previous years, the land beneath his feet, according to the red-headed document posted on the wall of the village cooperative, was now 'clearly allocated' for his family to cultivate. Of course, the lion's share of the harvest still had to go to the state, but at least, nominally, they had 'their own' land, instead of relying on the heavens and the whims of cadres for their yearly allotment.
His son, little Vasya, now almost as tall as Mikhail's shoulder, was no longer the little tyke who only knew to ask, 'Is life getting better?' He awkwardly followed his father, learning to sow a high-yield potato seed, supposedly 'scientifically cultivated.' The boy's strength had grown, and he could help quite a bit, though his movements were still clumsy, scattering seeds unevenly.
